title: TCHP: docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab and pertuzumab

agents.name: Docetaxel
agents.explanation: Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.
agents.watch: Take prescribed steroid premedication. Report fever, lasting numbness, swelling, sore nails or infusion symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and sepsis
Hair loss, mouth soreness and fatigue

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin creates links in DNA, making it harder for cells to copy and repair their genetic instructions. Its dose depends on kidney function as well as the intended regimen.
agents.watch: Keep blood-test appointments. Fever, unusual bleeding, repeated vomiting or infusion symptoms need prompt advice.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Allergic reaction, sometimes after previous exposure

agents.name: Trastuzumab
agents.explanation: Trastuzumab binds to the HER2 protein on cells and helps reduce HER2-driven growth and recruit immune activity. HER2 testing identifies the cancers for which this approach is used.
agents.watch: Attend planned echoes. Report breathlessness, ankle swelling, rapid weight gain or infusion symptoms.

agents.name: Pertuzumab
agents.mechanism: Blocks HER2 pairing with other receptors
agents.explanation: Pertuzumab binds a different area of HER2 from trastuzumab. It limits receptor pairing, so the two antibodies act together at different points on the same growth pathway.
agents.watch: Report diarrhoea early, especially with poor fluid intake. Keep cardiac checks and report infusion symptoms immediately.

context_label: HER2-positive early breast cancer · before surgery
purpose: TCHP aims to shrink HER2-positive breast cancer before surgery and reduce the risk of it returning.
schedule_summary: All four medicines are given by infusion on Day 1 of a 21-day cycle, for six cycles before surgery. Surgery findings guide the postoperative treatment. There is no routine take-home chemotherapy pump.

phases_note: A general pathway, not an appointment calendar. Your team confirms the order, overlap and duration; no date entry is needed.
timeline_note: Treatment bands show the source schedule. Symptom bands show possible patterns, not measured probabilities; serious effects can occur at any time.
safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override the timeline or diary.
teachback: Can you explain the current phase, which checks are expected next, and which symptoms mean you should call today? You do not need to enter dates to read the plan.
consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions, the planned monitoring and who to contact. Review the full longitudinal pathway and confirm which conditional treatments apply.
urgent_extra: Report new breathlessness, chest symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, jaundice, a painful swollen leg or a severe rash promptly. You do not need to identify which medicine caused the symptom.

questions.q: How does this fit around surgery and radiotherapy?
questions.a: Six cycles before surgery are one part of the pathway. Surgery findings determine the treatment afterwards; hormone treatment is added only if the cancer is also hormone-receptor positive.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. Both charts explain the expected sequence and general intervals without any dates or personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments.
The treatment journey lists baseline and ongoing checks, why they matter and what to ask. It does not mark tests as booked or completed.

questions.q: What happens if treatment is delayed?
questions.a: Your team may delay, reduce, change or stop a medicine. Ask which component changes and what happens to the next review; do not restart independently.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy or breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. The team should explain contraception and breastfeeding restrictions for every medicine, including how long precautions continue afterwards.

questions.q: How should I use trial numbers?
questions.a: Trial results describe groups with defined eligibility. Ask how well those patients and their treatment match your situation; the figures are not an individual prediction.

evidence.title: TRYPHAENA: interpreting early response
evidence.intro: The treatment setting, trial population and endpoint matter when interpreting benefit.
evidence.population: A randomised phase II study compared three neoadjuvant HER2-directed chemotherapy schedules, with cardiac safety as its main focus.
evidence.interpretation: One group received six cycles of TCHP. Pathological complete response means no residual invasive cancer in the assessed surgical tissue under the study definition; it is not a guarantee of cure. This study was not designed to establish a survival advantage between the three schedules.

items.title: Heart ultrasound (echo)
items.text: Before HER2 therapy; every 12 weeks during it; at completion. Checks heart pumping function, even without symptoms. Ask when the next echo is due and who arranges it. Report new breathlessness, swelling or palpitations.

items.title: Response and operation planning
items.text: During neoadjuvant treatment and before surgery. Checks the local response and helps plan surgery. Ask which breast imaging is planned and whether the result changes the operation.

items.title: Know the continuing plan
items.text: Annual mammography of remaining breast tissue after treatment; the team sets the first date. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. New symptoms need assessment between visits. Report new symptoms without waiting for the next mammogram.

items.title: Keep reporting symptoms
items.text: New or lasting symptoms need assessment between appointments and after treatment stops. Ask for a written summary of continuing medicines, follow-up tests and the contact plan.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, cardiac/immune checks as relevant, medicines review and the consent conversation come first.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Trained staff check and access the line, give the prescribed premedicines and infusions, and monitor for reactions. Tell the nurse immediately about pain, burning, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

anatomy: Hair loss or thinning varies. Ask about support and scalp cooling where appropriate.
Painful ulcers or difficulty eating and drinking need advice.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment.
Fainting, chest pain or severe breathing difficulty: urgent help. Keep scheduled cardiac checks.
Report diarrhoea early, especially with poor fluid intake, pain or fever.
Report lasting numbness, painful joints or difficulty with daily activities.
Fever, shivers or suddenly unwell: contact oncology immediately.
Severe rash, blistering or yellow skin/eyes needs prompt advice.
